lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.intro: In France, a greeting isn't optional small talk — it's the expected first step before any interaction, even a quick one in a shop.
lessons.didYouKnow: Walking into a small shop, café, or even a doctor's waiting room without saying "Bonjour" first is considered genuinely rude — it's expected before you ask for anything, not after.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into English or a question without saying "Bonjour" first — it noticeably changes how you're received, even if the rest of the conversation ends up in English.

quiz.question: What should you say before asking a shopkeeper a question in France?

lessons.title: Emergency Phrases
lessons.intro: Quick phrases worth having ready before you land.
lessons.didYouKnow: France's general emergency number is 112 (EU-wide) — 15 is specifically for medical emergencies (SAMU) and 17 for police, but 112 works for any of them.
commonMistakes: Not knowing 112 works from any phone, even without a French SIM or credit.

quiz.question: What's the general EU emergency number that also works in France?

lessons.title: Café Culture
lessons.intro: A French café isn't a quick-service coffee shop — it's a place to sit, linger, and be left alone by the waiter, which surprises visitors expecting fast table turnover.
lessons.didYouKnow: Once you're seated, a table is considered yours for as long as you like — waiters generally won't rush you or bring the check unprompted, since lingering over one coffee for an hour is completely normal.
commonMistakes: Waiting for the check to be brought automatically — like in much of Europe, you need to ask for it, or you may sit long after you're done.

quiz.question: In a French café, when will the check usually arrive?
options: Only when you ask for it
You pay at a register on the way in

lessons.title: Dining Etiquette
lessons.intro: French restaurant service follows some specific customs around tipping, bread, and pacing that are easy to get wrong without knowing them in advance.
lessons.didYouKnow: A service charge ("service compris") is legally included in the listed price at French restaurants — an additional large tip isn't expected, though rounding up or leaving a few euros for great service is appreciated.
commonMistakes: Tipping 15-20% like in the US — service is already included in the price, so a large additional tip isn't the norm.
Asking for substitutions or major modifications to a dish — French kitchens generally expect you to order as menu'd.

quiz.question: What does "service compris" mean on a French bill?
options: The meal comes with free wine

lessons.title: Metro Etiquette
lessons.intro: The Paris metro (and French trains generally) move fast and have their own unwritten rules — a couple of them trip up almost every first-time visitor.
lessons.didYouKnow: On regional and intercity trains (though not the Paris metro itself), paper tickets historically needed to be validated ("composter") at a small machine before boarding — check current signage, since this has been changing, but it's worth knowing about.

phrases.text: Où est la station la plus proche?
phrases.pronunciation: oo eh lah stah-SYOHN lah ploo PROHSH

commonMistakes: Blocking the doors while people are trying to exit before you board — French commuters move fast and expect you to step aside and let people off first.

quiz.question: What should you do before boarding a crowded metro car?
options: Let people exit first, then board
Wait for the next train always

lessons.title: Shopping Etiquette
lessons.intro: Shopping in France, especially at smaller boutiques, comes with the same greeting-first etiquette as any other interaction.
lessons.didYouKnow: Browsing without acknowledging the shopkeeper, or picking items up without asking in smaller boutiques, can come across as impolite — a greeting and a bit of a rapport is expected, even if you're just browsing.
commonMistakes: Walking into a small boutique and browsing silently without greeting the shopkeeper — say "Bonjour" on the way in, same as anywhere else in France.

quiz.question: What should you do when entering a small French boutique?
options: Say nothing until you're ready to buy
Wait to be greeted first, always
